passage: You asked what night shift at the call centre really feels like, Usha. That first month, I felt like I was underwater. I worked ten at night to seven in the morning. I'd come home, eat breakfast while everyone else was leaving, then lie awake with sunlight leaking through the curtains and the pressure cooker going off. By afternoon I was foggy, teary for no reason, snapping at my little brother. I missed my cousin's engagement because I was asleep. What helped? Two things. Papa pinned a thick dark sheet over my window, and I started sleeping the same hours every day, even on off days. And I finally sat the family down and stuck my schedule on the fridge. My name is Seema, and now my whole family whispers till two. Mostly.

qa.q: What did Seema's Papa pin over the window?
qa.a: A thick dark sheet.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling in the afternoons of that first month?
qa.a: Seema felt foggy, low and teary, out of step with the family, which showed in snapping at the little brother.

qa.q: What changes helped Seema, and why?
qa.a: Sleeping the same hours in a darkened room and sharing the schedule with the family, so the body could settle and everyone knew when to keep quiet.

qa.q: How might Seema's little brother have seen those first weeks?
qa.a: The little brother probably found Seema grumpy and hard to be around, snapped at for no clear reason, without knowing it came from broken sleep.

grounding: Shows a young adult on night shifts feeling foggy, low and out of step with family life, helped by consistent sleep hours in a dark room and honesty about the schedule.

passage: I'm Keerthana, Sumit's older sister, and since he started nights at the warehouse I barely see him. He comes in at six in the morning, when Maa is packing tiffins, and sits blinking at his tea as if he's forgotten how to drink it. He missed Maa's birthday lunch because he was asleep, and afterwards sat on the steps looking so low that I didn't dare tease him. Last week he did something new. He taped foil over his window, asked us to keep the radio off until two, and wrote his sleep hours on the kitchen calendar. 'Please don't wake me unless it's urgent,' he said. I think it's helping. He laughed at dinner yesterday.

qa.q: What did Sumit tape over his window?
qa.a: Foil.

qa.q: What does Sumit sitting on the steps after missing the birthday lunch suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed low and guilty about missing Maa's birthday, worn down by a body clock out of step with the family.

qa.q: What helped Sumit, and why?
qa.a: Darkening the room, fixing his sleep hours on the calendar and telling the family plainly, so he could sleep properly and they knew when to be quiet.

qa.q: What is it like for Keerthana to live with Sumit's night shifts?
qa.a: She misses him and isn't sure how to act around him, but she notices small signs, like his laugh at dinner, that things are getting better.

grounding: Shows, through a sister's eyes, a young adult on night shifts who is foggy, low and out of step with family life, and who helps himself with fixed sleep hours in a dark room and honesty about his schedule.

passage:
Sunaina: Bhaiya, you missed Maa's birthday cake again 😔
Manoj: I know. Shift ended at 6, slept till 3. My head is fog.
Sunaina: You snapped at everyone at lunch yesterday too
Manoj: Sorry. Everything feels flat lately. Like I live in a different time zone from you all.
Sunaina: Can we fix it?
Manoj: My supervisor said keep the same sleep hours every day, even on off days. And a dark room.
Sunaina: I'll stitch a thick curtain from Nani's old sari.
Manoj: And I'll tell Maa my schedule properly so she stops waking me for lunch.
Sunaina: Deal. Saturday dinner at 8, before your shift?
Manoj: Put it in the family group. I'll be there.

qa.q: What will Sunaina stitch the curtain from?
qa.a: From Nani's old sari.

qa.q: How is Manoj feeling during these night-shift weeks?
qa.a: He feels foggy, flat and out of step with the family, and sorry for snapping at everyone.

qa.q: What two changes did Manoj plan?
qa.a: Keeping the same sleep hours every day in a dark room, and telling Maa his schedule properly.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina when Manoj misses family moments?
qa.a: Sunaina feels sad and let down, but she still wants to help him fix it.

grounding: A young man on night shifts feels foggy and low, and a steady sleep window, a dark room and honesty with family help.

passage: Varun had taken the night watchman's job at the sugar mill outside Kopargaon to pay for his diploma. By the third week the village had turned upside down for him. At noon, when his body begged for sleep, the rooster, the flour mill and his nephews' cricket shook the house. He ate lunch at dawn and dinner at noon, felt dull and sad for no clear reason, and barely spoke. His sister Jahnavi found him staring at the wall. 'Tell us what you need,' she said. He covered the back-room window with a gunny sack, kept the same sleeping hours even on Sundays, and pinned his shift chart by the kitchen. The nephews moved their cricket to the field.

qa.q: What did Varun use to cover the back-room window?
qa.a: A gunny sack.

qa.q: How did Varun feel by the third week of night shifts?
qa.a: He felt dull and sad without knowing why, and so drained that he barely spoke.

qa.q: Why did pinning his shift chart by the kitchen help?
qa.a: It told the family honestly when he slept, so they could keep the noise away and his days became steadier.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt seeing Varun stare at the wall?
qa.a: She was probably worried about him and wanted to help, which is why she asked what he needed.

grounding: A young night watchman fights his body clock and low mood, and a dark room, fixed sleep and an open schedule help.

passage: In Busan, Soo-ah stacked bread trays at a bakery factory from ten at night until six. She got home just as her flatmate Jana left for class, and the two of them passed like trains. After a month Soo-ah felt her thoughts moving through syrup. She cried over a spilled coffee and forgot her mother's call twice. Jana left a note on the fridge: 'Worried about you. Talk tonight?' They talked over Soo-ah's breakfast, which was Jana's dinner. Soo-ah put up blackout blinds, slept the same hours every day, and messaged her mother her schedule. On Sundays she and Jana now share a real lunch at noon.

qa.q: What did Jana write on the note on the fridge?
qa.a: 'Worried about you. Talk tonight?'

qa.q: What does Soo-ah crying over a spilled coffee suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt worn out and low; the night shifts had left her mood fragile.

qa.q: Which steps helped Soo-ah?
qa.a: Blackout blinds, sleeping the same hours every day, and telling her mother her schedule.

qa.q: How might Jana have experienced the month of passing like trains?
qa.a: Jana probably felt worried and a little lonely, missing the flatmate and noticing the change.

grounding: A young night-shift worker feels foggy and low, and a dark room, steady sleep hours and honesty about the schedule help.

passage: At 3 a.m. the call centre in Gurugram hummed under white lights, and Jeevan realised he had read the same customer's address three times. It was his sixth week on nights. His days had turned upside down: he slept in scraps between his sister's school run and the pressure-cooker whistles, missed Sunday lunch, and snapped when Ammi asked why he was "always sleeping". During the break his team lead, Rehana, found him staring at the vending machine. "You look grey. What are your sleep hours?" "Whenever the house is quiet." "Then fix them. Same hours every day, even on days off, and dark curtains. And tell your family the timetable, so they're not guessing." That weekend Jeevan stuck a paper on the fridge: "Sleeping 9 to 4. Wake me only for fire." Ammi laughed and put the pressure cooker on at five.

qa.q: What did Jeevan write on the paper on the fridge?
qa.a: "Sleeping 9 to 4. Wake me only for fire."

qa.q: How was Jeevan feeling in his sixth week on nights, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt foggy, low and irritable; he read an address three times and snapped at Ammi.

qa.q: What advice from Rehana helps with the night-shift body clock?
qa.a: Keeping the same sleep hours every day, using dark curtains, and telling the family the timetable.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt before and after the note on the fridge?
qa.a: Before, she was probably puzzled or worried by his constant sleeping; after, she understood and happily fitted the cooking around it.

grounding: Shows a young adult on night shifts feeling foggy, low and out of step with family, and fixed sleep hours in a dark room plus honesty about the schedule helping.
